title: Input Capture: Web Portal Capture
summary: Web portal capture plants credential recording code on an externally facing login page so that usernames and passwords are saved or forwarded before the service authenticates the user. The page normally keeps working, which is why the compromise can survive for a long time: users sign in successfully and see nothing wrong. Access to the page may come from exploitation of the externally facing web service during initial compromise, or from legitimate administrative access used after an earlier intrusion as a backup way to keep remote access alive. Because targets are often virtual private network portals or webmail front ends, a successful capture yields accounts that reach deep into the internal network. Detection depends on file integrity monitoring of web content, review of web server and application logs for unexpected code paths or outbound requests, comparison of deployed pages against a known good baseline, and authentication records showing logins from client software or locations that differ from the victim's normal pattern.

beginner.definition: Web portal capture means changing a login page on a company website so that it copies what people type. The page still works normally, so users sign in and see nothing strange at all. The attacker then holds real usernames and passwords. This often targets a remote access page, because accounts created there can reach a great deal of the network.
beginner.whyItMatters: A remote access login page is a doorway into the whole network, so the details typed there are extremely valuable. Because the page keeps working, users and administrators may not notice anything for months. The attacker never needs to break a password, since people hand over working ones themselves. Reviewing the code behind a page rarely happens once a site is live. This makes web portal capture a quiet and powerful way to keep access.
howItWorks: The company publishes a login page so that staff can reach services from outside.
An attacker gains the ability to change the files that build that login page.
Extra code is added that copies the username and password as they are submitted.
The copied details are written to a file or sent to a server the attacker controls.
The login page then continues normally, so the user reaches the service as expected.
Administrators may also add this recording after an earlier break in to keep access.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk that signs guests in and writes each name into a book. Someone quietly adds a second, hidden page inside that same book. Guests still sign once, still receive their room key, and the desk still works exactly as usual. But every name and room number is copied onto the hidden page, which is later torn out and taken away. The hotel's own records look complete and correct, so nobody thinks to check the binding.
takeaways: A working and trusted login page can still be stealing credentials.
Remote access portals are attractive targets because their accounts reach far.
Compare live web content against a known good copy, not only against error logs.

objectives: Explain how credential recording code is added to a live login page.
Describe why a captured portal credential is especially valuable to an attacker.
Identify file integrity and log evidence of modified web content.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from a lookalike fake login site.
Describe monitoring that would reveal captured credentials leaving the server.
